Solids, Liquids and Gases: Matter is usually found as a solid, a liquid or a gas. A solid has a definite shape and volume because its particles are packed closely and vibrate in fixed positions. A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container because its particles are close but can slide past each other. A gas has no definite shape or volume because its particles are far apart and move freely, so gases are easily compressed. Plasma, the state of very hot ionized gas, is found in stars and lightning. Particles in all states are in constant motion.
Kinetic Molecular Theory: The kinetic molecular theory states that all matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion. The particles of a gas move quickly in straight lines and collide with each other and with the walls of the container; those collisions cause gas pressure. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles: the hotter the substance, the faster its particles move. In a solid the attractions between particles are strongest and in a gas they are weakest. Heating a substance gives its particles more energy until they overcome the attractions and the state changes.
Changes of State: A change of state is a physical change. Melting is solid to liquid, freezing is liquid to solid, vaporization is liquid to gas, condensation is gas to liquid, sublimation is solid directly to gas and deposition is gas directly to solid. Vaporization happens by evaporation at the surface at any temperature or by boiling throughout the liquid at the boiling point. Melting and freezing occur at the melting point, 0 degrees C for water. Water boils at 100 degrees C at sea level. Energy is absorbed in melting and vaporization and released in freezing and condensation.
Heating and Cooling Curves: A heating curve graphs temperature against time as a substance is heated at a constant rate. Sloped sections show the temperature rising while the substance is a solid, liquid or gas; the energy increases the kinetic energy of the particles. Flat sections show a change of state: the temperature stays constant because the added energy is used to overcome the attractions between particles, not to raise the temperature. For water the flat sections are at 0 degrees C (melting) and 100 degrees C (boiling), and the boiling plateau is longer because vaporization needs more energy. A cooling curve is the reverse.
Thermal Energy, Temperature and Heat: Thermal energy is the total kinetic energy of all the particles of a substance, so it depends on the amount of matter as well as the temperature. Temperature is the average kinetic energy of the particles. Heat is the transfer of thermal energy from a hotter object to a colder one. Heat is transferred by conduction (direct contact), convection (moving fluids) and radiation (electromagnetic waves, needing no medium). The heat needed to change the temperature of a mass m by an amount delta T is Q = m c delta T, where c is the specific heat capacity; water has c = 4200 J/(kg C). Metals are good conductors and gases are poor conductors.
